title: The pool that never empties
prompt: A pool holds 100 ETH and 200,000 USDC under x*y=k. A trader buys 10 ETH. Ignoring fees, how much USDC do they pay?
hint: k must stay the same after the trade. Solve for the USDC balance when 90 ETH are left.
explain: k = 20,000,000. With 90 ETH left, USDC must be 222,222. The trader paid 22,222. Big trades on small pools get expensive fast.

title: Average is not spot
prompt: A pool holds 50 ETH and 100,000 USDC, so ETH is quoted at 2,000. A trader buys 5 ETH in one swap, no fees. What average price per ETH did they pay, in USDC?
hint: Find the USDC balance after the trade using x*y=k, then divide what they paid by 5.
explain: k = 5,000,000. With 45 ETH left the pool needs 111,111 USDC, so the trader paid 11,111 for 5 ETH: 2,222 each. That gap to spot is price impact.

title: Pick the tier
prompt: An LP wants to provide USDC/USDT liquidity in Uniswap v3. Which fee tier will attract the volume?
hint: Two dollar-pegged tokens barely move against each other. What would a trader pay for that?
explain: Stable pairs live in the 0.01% tier. Anything higher and traders route around you. Volatile pairs justify 0.3% or 1%.

title: Ticks to double
prompt: In v3 each tick moves price by 0.01%: price at tick i is 1.0001^i. Roughly how many ticks lie between a price and double that price?
hint: You need 1.0001^n = 2. Take logarithms: n = ln 2 / ln 1.0001.
explain: ln 2 is 0.6931 and ln 1.0001 is about 0.0001, so about 6,931 ticks. A price doubling is a long walk in tick space.

title: The LP who did nothing
prompt: You LP ETH/USDC across the full range. ETH doubles. Compared with simply holding the same starting tokens, how far behind is the LP position, before fees?
hint: The LP value grows with the square root of the price ratio. Compare 2 x sqrt(2) with 1 + 2.
explain: LP value is proportional to 2 x sqrt(2) = 2.83, holding is worth 3. That is 5.7% behind: impermanent loss. Fees have to beat it.

title: The cheapest transaction
prompt: How much gas does a plain ETH transfer with no data cost on Ethereum?
hint: It is the constant every gas estimator starts from.
explain: 21,000 gas. Every contract call costs at least that plus whatever the code does.

title: Watching the chain
prompt: Standup starts at 09:00 and you promise to watch mainnet for exactly 30 blocks. Blocks arrive every 12 seconds. When can you stop?
hint: Multiply blocks by seconds, then convert to minutes.
explain: 30 x 12 seconds = 360 seconds = 6 minutes. 09:06. Ethereum is boringly regular since the merge.

title: Confirmed, or is it
prompt: Your deploy shows 'confirmed' at the newest block. A colleague says the transaction could still vanish. Who is right?
choices: Neither: confirmations do not exist post-merge
Both: it depends on the gas price
Your colleague: a reorg can drop recent blocks until finality
hint: Think about what happens when two validators propose competing blocks.
explain: Recent blocks can be reorganised until the chain finalises them, about two epochs (13 minutes) later. 'Confirmed' means included, not final.

title: Minimum out
prompt: You swap 10,000 USDC, quoted 5 ETH, with slippage tolerance 0.5%. What is the minimum ETH out you will accept, in thousandths of an ETH?
hint: Take 0.5% off the quote, then express it in milli-ETH.
explain: 5 ETH x 0.995 = 4.975 ETH, so 4,975 milli-ETH. If the pool moves more than that before inclusion, the swap reverts instead of overpaying.

title: Three transactions
prompt: In one block, in order: address A buys ETH, then your ETH buy, then address A sells ETH. What just happened to you?
choices: A sandwich attack: A pushed the price up, you bought high, A sold into you
hint: Look at who profits from your trade executing at a worse price.
explain: Classic sandwich. A front-ran your buy and back-ran it. Tight slippage limits and private order flow are the defences.

title: Proof length
prompt: An airdrop claim contract stores 1,048,576 eligible addresses as leaves of a balanced Merkle tree. How many hashes does one claim proof contain?
hint: 1,048,576 is a power of two. The proof has one sibling hash per level.
explain: 1,048,576 = 2^20, so the tree has 20 levels and each proof carries 20 sibling hashes. A million claims, 640 bytes of proof each.

title: Dead beef
prompt: 0xdead + 0xbeef = ?
hint: Convert both to decimal, add, convert back. Or add hex column by column with carries.
explain: 57,005 + 48,879 = 105,884 = 0x19d9c. Engineers who read calldata for fun do this in their heads. Nobody else needs to.

title: Two days
prompt: A Uniswap governance proposal passes. Voting ends Friday at 15:00 and the Timelock delay is 2 days. When is the earliest it can execute?
hint: The delay is measured from when the proposal is queued, not from the next working day.
explain: Sunday 15:00. The timelock exists so everyone can see what is coming. It does not care about weekends.

title: The quorum
prompt: UNI has a total supply of 1,000,000,000 tokens and proposals need 4% of supply voting in favour to reach quorum. How many million UNI is that?
hint: Four percent of a billion.
explain: 40 million UNI. Proposals fail for lack of quorum more often than for opposition.

title: The loop
prompt: Code review: for (uint i = 0; i <= holders.length; i++) { pay(holders[i]); }  What is wrong?
choices: The <= reads one past the end of the array and reverts
hint: Arrays with length n have indices 0 to n minus 1.
explain: Off by one. holders[holders.length] is out of bounds and Solidity reverts the whole payout. The oldest bug there is.

title: Send, then update
prompt: A contract sends ETH to the caller and only afterwards sets their balance to zero. What is the classic risk?
choices: Reentrancy: the receiver calls back in and withdraws again before the balance is zeroed
hint: What can a contract do when it receives ETH?
explain: Reentrancy, as in The DAO. The receiving contract's fallback calls withdraw again while the balance still reads full.

title: The right order
prompt: Which order of operations does the checks-effects-interactions pattern prescribe inside a function?
hint: Do all your own bookkeeping before you talk to any other contract.
explain: Validate inputs, update your own state, and only then call out. External calls last, so a callback finds your state already settled.

title: Settle at the end
prompt: In Uniswap v4 a single contract holds every pool and tracks token deltas during a transaction, requiring only the net amounts to be paid at the end. What is this pattern called?
hint: It uses transient storage that only lives for one transaction.
explain: Flash accounting. Multi-hop swaps move tokens once instead of at every hop, which is most of v4's gas savings.

title: Before and after
prompt: What v4 feature lets a pool run custom code before and after swaps, liquidity changes and donations?
hint: The pool's address encodes which callbacks it wants.
explain: Hooks. Dynamic fees, limit orders, TWAMM, KYC pools: all hooks attached to otherwise standard pools.

title: Approve once
prompt: Which Uniswap contract lets a user approve a token once and then authorise many apps to spend it with signatures instead of new approval transactions?
hint: The name says what it does, and it is the second attempt at it.
explain: Permit2. It brings permit-style signatures to every ERC-20, including the ones that never implemented EIP-2612.

title: Spacing
prompt: In Uniswap v3 the 0.3% fee tier has a fixed tick spacing. What is it?
hint: 0.05% uses 10, 1% uses 200. The middle tier sits between them.
explain: 60. Positions in that tier can only start and end on ticks divisible by 60, which keeps swaps cheap.

title: The receipt
prompt: Gas price 20 gwei, the transaction used 100,000 gas. What did it cost, in thousandths of an ETH?
hint: 1 gwei is a billionth of an ETH. Multiply, then convert.
explain: 20 gwei x 100,000 = 2,000,000 gwei = 0.002 ETH, so 2 thousandths. Cheap day.

title: What you actually pay
prompt: Base fee is 30 gwei. You set a max priority fee of 2 gwei and a max fee of 50 gwei. What do you pay per gas?
hint: You pay base fee plus tip, as long as that is under your max.
explain: Base 30 plus tip 2 = 32 gwei. The unused 18 gwei of headroom is refunded. The 30 is burned, the 2 goes to the validator.

title: Who pairs with Ana
prompt: Ana always pairs with whoever reviewed her last PR. Ben never reviews on Mondays. Cai reviewed Ana's last PR on Friday. It is Monday. Who pairs with Ana?
hint: Only one fact decides the pairing. The others are noise.
explain: Cai. Ben's Monday habit is irrelevant, which is the point of the puzzle. Standups are full of irrelevant facts.

title: PR four thousand
prompt: Pull request #4096 merges. The release bot prints PR numbers in binary. How many digits does it print?
hint: 4096 is a power of two. How many zeros follow the 1?
explain: 4096 = 2^12 = 1 followed by twelve zeros: 13 digits. The bot's author regrets the joke.

title: The allowance race
prompt: A user lowers a spender's ERC-20 allowance from 100 to 50 in a single approve transaction. Why might the spender end up with 150?
choices: The spender front-runs: spends the 100, then the new 50 lands
hint: Think about what the spender can do while the approve is waiting in the mempool.
explain: Front-running. The spender sees the approve pending, spends the old 100, then spends the new 50. Use increase and decrease allowance, or Permit2.

title: The stubborn oracle
prompt: Which price is the hardest for an attacker to manipulate within a single block?
choices: The price on a centralised exchange API
hint: Moving an average requires holding the price there for a long time, and that costs.
explain: The TWAP. To move a 30-minute average by 10% you must hold the spot price 10% off for 30 minutes, and every arbitrageur gets paid to stop you.

title: Seven tokens, three LPs
prompt: A contract splits 7 tokens equally among 3 LPs using Solidity integer math. What happens?
choices: Each gets 2 and 1 token stays in the contract
Each gets 3 and the contract mints 2
hint: Solidity has no decimals. Division rounds toward zero.
explain: 7 / 3 = 2 with remainder 1. Each LP gets 2 and the leftover token is stuck unless the code handles dust. Most audits find at least one of these.

title: Two LPs, one price
prompt: ETH trades at 2,000. LP A provides 1,000 to 4,000, LP B provides 1,900 to 2,100 with the same capital. While the price sits at 2,000, who earns more fees?
choices: B: the same capital is concentrated where the trades happen
Neither, fees only accrue on withdrawal
hint: Fees are shared by liquidity active at the current tick, not by capital deposited.
explain: B, by a lot. Concentrated liquidity means B's capital is many times denser at 2,000. The price leaving B's range is the catch.

title: Left behind
prompt: An LP provides ETH/USDC between 1,900 and 2,100. ETH rallies to 2,300. What does the position now hold?
hint: As price rises through the range, traders buy the position's ETH.
explain: Only USDC. The position sold its ETH on the way up and now earns nothing until the price comes back. Ranges need tending.

title: Faster blocks
prompt: Unichain produces a block every second. How many Unichain blocks land during one 12-second Ethereum block?
hint: Divide the slow chain's block time by the fast chain's.
explain: 12. Faster blocks mean faster confirmation for swaps, and more blocks for a sandwich bot to think about.

title: Permission bits
prompt: A v4 hook's permissions are encoded in the low bits of its address. A hook has the flags at bits 0, 2 and 3 set. What is that flag value in decimal?
hint: Bit n is worth 2 to the power n. Add them up.
explain: 1 + 4 + 8 = 13. Hook developers mine addresses until the low bits match the callbacks they implement.

title: Standup in Bangkok
prompt: Standup is 09:00 in New York, which is on daylight time (UTC-4). You are in Bangkok (UTC+7). When is standup for you?
hint: Convert New York to UTC first, then add Bangkok's offset.
explain: 09:00 EDT = 13:00 UTC = 20:00 in Bangkok. Dinner standup. The nomad's daily arithmetic.

title: Hash size
prompt: How many bytes long is a keccak256 hash?
hint: 256 bits.
explain: 32 bytes, 64 hex characters. Every storage slot, address derivation and Merkle leaf leans on it.

title: The square root
prompt: Uniswap v3 stores price as sqrt(price) scaled by 2^96. If the stored value represents sqrt(price) = 2, what is the price?
hint: Undo the square root.
explain: 4. Storing the square root makes the liquidity math linear. It also makes every off-by-2^96 bug spectacular.

title: Passes at home, fails in CI
prompt: A test passes on your laptop and fails in CI, but only when CI runs around 00:00 UTC. What is the likely bug?
choices: A date or timezone boundary: 'today' differs between the two machines
hint: What changes about the world at exactly midnight UTC?
explain: A day-boundary bug. Your laptop is in a different timezone, so 'today' differs from CI's around midnight. Mock the clock.

title: Whose gas
prompt: You bridge 1 ETH to an L2 and swap it there. Which chain's gas do you pay for the swap?
choices: Neither, swaps on L2 are free
hint: The swap executes where the pool lives.
explain: The L2's. The L2 then pays mainnet to post the data, which is why L2 fees rise when mainnet is busy.

title: Falling price
prompt: In UniswapX an order starts at a price good for the swapper and decays over time until a filler accepts it. What kind of auction is that?
hint: Named after the flower markets that price downwards.
explain: A Dutch auction. Fillers compete to accept as soon as the price is profitable for them, which is what gets the swapper a good price.
